sceneHappening: Love: the more excellent way that makes every gift worth something
summary: Paul says that if he speaks in the tongues of men and of angels but has not love, he is a noisy gong or clanging cymbal. If he has prophecy, knows all mysteries and all knowledge, has all faith to move mountains, gives away all he has, even hands over his body to be burned, but has not love, he gains nothing. Then he describes love: it is patient and kind; it does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude; it does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. "Love never fails." Prophecies will pass away, tongues will cease, knowledge will pass away, for we know in part and prophesy in part; when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away. When Paul was a child, he spoke, thought, and reasoned like a child; when he became a man, he put childish ways behind him. "For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I also am fully known." "But now faith, hope, and love remain, these three. The greatest of these is love."
whySettingMatters: This chapter is often read alone, as a poem for weddings, but it sits in the middle of Paul's argument about spiritual gifts in chapters 12 to 14. The Corinthians prized tongues, knowledge, and spiritual status, and Paul says that without love these are worth nothing. Each line of the description of love can be read as a contrast with Corinthian behavior: they were jealous, boastful, arrogant, insisting on their rights, and quick to take offense. The "mirror" (13:12) in a Greek city like Corinth, famous for bronze work, was polished metal, which gave a blurred reflection, so "seeing dimly" is a good picture of present knowledge. "When the perfect comes" (13:10) is debated: most read it as the final coming of Christ, when we see face to face, while others think it refers to the completion of the church or of Scripture; the surrounding verses about "face to face" fit the first better. The chapter does not say that gifts are bad, only that they are partial and temporary and that love is permanent.

people.note: Describes the way of love, using himself as an example.
Eager for gifts, and called to love.

questions: Paul lists impressive acts, including martyrdom, and says they are worthless without love. What does that say about how we measure faithfulness?
Read the description of love as a mirror for the Corinthians' behavior. Which lines hit hardest?
"We know in part." How does that help in disagreements about what is true or important?
Why is love "the greatest" of faith, hope, and love?

words.note: "If I have the gift of prophecy" (13:2, 13:8).
"If I speak with the languages of men and of angels" (13:1, 13:8).
"When that which is perfect has come" (13:10).
"Then I will know fully, even as I was fully known" (13:12).
